sources.title: Palawa Story
sources.note: Aboriginal Land Council of Tasmania community account of Country, invasion, survival, families, political action and living Palawa continuity.

sources.title: Aboriginal Life Pre-Invasion
sources.note: University of Tasmania synthesis by Patsy Cameron on seasonal movement, foods, women, shelters, fire, tools, language groups, ceremony and exchange.

sources.title: Aboriginal Heritage of the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area
sources.note: Australian government archaeological literature synthesis covering dated caves, fauna, bone and stone tools, rock markings, occupation and evidence limits.

sources.title: Aboriginal Heritage in Tasmania Parks
sources.note: Tasmanian Parks account of deep occupation, varied cultural landscapes, targeted burning, intangible heritage and continuing custodianship.

sources.title: Aboriginal Cultural Values in the Tasmanian Wilderness World Heritage Area
sources.note: Aboriginal Heritage Tasmania account of dated rockshelters, small hand stencils, hut depressions, shell middens and living cultural value.

sources.title: Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Site Types
sources.note: Tasmanian government definitions and cautions for middens, markings, shelters, burning, artefacts, burials, huts, arrangements and quarries.

sources.title: Aboriginal Quarries
sources.note: Tasmanian government evidence for stone and ochre quarrying, material selection, exchange networks, processing and continuing ochre practice.

sources.title: Aboriginal Shell Middens
sources.note: Tasmanian government archaeology of shell deposits, food processing, technology, seasonality, environmental adaptation and legal protection.

sources.title: Aboriginal Rock Markings
sources.note: Aboriginal Heritage Tasmania explanation of pecked and ground markings, repeated visits, possible functions, lost meanings and community reconnection.

sources.title: The Orb: Shelters
sources.note: Community-centered Tasmanian education resource on rockshelters, lean-tos, dome huts, communal places and intergenerational shelter-making knowledge.

sources.title: The Orb: Stone Tools
sources.note: Community-centered Tasmanian education resource on quarry sites, knapping, stone-tool knowledge and modern Aboriginal skill renewal.

sources.title: Tasmanian Archaeology: Establishing the Sequences
sources.note: Peer-reviewed review of cave and midden sequences, changing coastal food strategies, disputed explanations and rejection of frozen Paleolithic stereotypes.

sources.title: Lithic Technology in Tasmania
sources.note: Peer-reviewed eastern and southern Tasmanian study showing the need to analyze manufacturing techniques rather than rank apparently simple tools.

sources.title: Visions of the Australian Pleistocene: Lake Mungo and Kutikina
sources.note: Australian Archaeology study separating excavated Kutikina stone, bone and fire evidence from invented details in popular reconstruction art.

sources.title: The Polemics of Making Fire in Tasmania
sources.note: University of Tasmania repository article showing ambiguity in historical claims about fire-making and warning against degeneration narratives.

sources.title: Aboriginal Organisation
sources.note: University of Tasmania account of extended families and hearth groups as social foundations, plus family continuity through colonial disruption.

sources.title: Aboriginal Traditional Diet
sources.note: University of Tasmania synthesis of environmental change, managed foods, animals, shellfish, plants and later disruption of food systems.

sources.title: Tasmanian Aboriginal Shell Necklaces
sources.note: National Museum account of women’s seasonal collecting, processing, exchange, intergenerational teaching, archaeological pierced shells and cultural continuity.

sources.title: Tasmanian Bark Canoe
sources.note: National Museum account of documented watercraft uses and Rex Greeno’s explicitly modern family reconstruction and knowledge transmission.

sources.title: Tuylini Stringybark Canoe
sources.note: Tasmanian Museum account of bundled bark or reed construction, regional materials, island travel, carried hearths and modern revival evidence.

sources.title: Rikawa: Tasmanian Aboriginal Kelp Water Containers
sources.note: Peer-reviewed community and museum collaboration on historic kelp vessels, women’s making, fresh-water transport, material analysis and revived practice.

sources.title: About Palawa Kani
sources.note: Tasmanian Aboriginal Centre account of original language records, recorder problems, community-led reconstruction, teaching and present spoken use.

sources.title: A Voyage to the Pacific Ocean, Volume I
sources.note: Digitized 1784 primary account preserving William Anderson’s January 1777 Adventure Bay word list and the encounter’s recording limitations.

sources.title: Palawa Kani and the Value of Language in Aboriginal Tasmania
sources.note: Peer-reviewed history of the nine Anderson words, fragmentary colonial wordlists, lost grammatical context and modern language renewal.

sources.title: Exploration by Sea
sources.note: University of Tasmania chronology of Tasman, the fatal 1772 French encounter, Furneaux, Cook and later transient maritime visits.

sources.title: The Black Line
sources.note: National Museum history of first recorded contact, post-1803 invasion, violence, dispossession and the coercive 1830 colonial campaign.

sources.title: Ningina Tunapri
sources.note: Tasmanian Museum gallery centered on more than two thousand generations of cultural continuance and living Tasmanian Aboriginal custodianship.

sources.title: Putalina, Oyster Cove
sources.note: National Museum community and object history of forced displacement, continued making, 1984 reoccupation, 1995 land return and celebration.

proposedOverrides.summary: Plural Tasmanian Aboriginal histories and living Palawa continuity.

batchIdentityNotes: The imported label is treated as an atlas category, not a self-name, single nation, language, economy, polity or uniform hunter-gatherer culture.
The exact 40-position polygon omits tested northern, coastal and Bass Strait places important to Tasmanian Aboriginal history; its geometry is not endorsed as Country.
The target vanishes at 300 BCE beneath a broad Australian category and returns at 200 BCE with its former hash; the gap is editorial, not demographic.
At 1783 another exact id, aboriginal-tasmanians-1783, takes over a near-matching polygon. The switch is taxonomy, not extinction or state succession.
Living Palawa peoples and institutions are continuous and distinct from all imported atlas labels. Later community practice appears with its own date and attribution.

A securely dated 1777 Adventure Bay vocabulary permits one tiny contemporaneous language record, Teegera recorded as to eat. It is European transcription, not Indigenous writing or an island-wide language sample.
